results.title: Sample size and power calculations made simple
results.content: Background Sample size estimation is an important concern for researchers as guidelines must be adhered to for ethics committees, grant applications and publications. Content The process of sample size calculations, including relevant definitions, is explained and clear examples for different study designs are provided for illustration. Conclusions The information regarding sample sizes and statistical programs should be useful for researchers in order to perform sample size calculations for research projects. Background: Sample size estimation is an important concern for researchers as guidelines. According to the literature, the minimal number for pilot research is 10; hence the sample size for the study was taken in light of this information (McCrum-Gardner, 2010). It is frequently used in undergraduate and cross-sectional studies in health sciences and education due to its practical nature and standard statistical assumptions (McCrum-Gardner, 2010 and generalizability should consider more advanced power analysis methods to determine the optimal sample size. Power, effect and sample size using GPower: Practical issues for researchers and members of research ethics committees. Aim. To enable researchers and research ethics committee members with non-statistical backgrounds to use freely available statistical software to explore and address issues relating to sample size, effect size and power. The examples illustrate the importance of effect and sample size in optimising the probability of a study to detect treatment effects, without requiring these effects to be massive. Researchers and research ethics committee members need to be familiar with the technicalities of sample size estimation in order to make informed judgements on sample size, power of tests and associated ethical issues. Health care researchers should carefully consider each of the aspects inherent in sample size estimations. Sample-size determination is often an important step in planning a statistical study---and it is usually a difficult one. Also discussed is the possibility that sample size may not be the main issue, that the real goal is to design a high-quality study. Key words: Power; Sample size; Observed power; Retrospective power; Study design; Cohen's effect measures; Equivalence testing; # I wish to thank Kate Cowles, John Castelloe, Steve Simon, two referees, an editor, and an associate editor for their helpful comments on earlier drafts of this paper.
